$comment: Shared module-lane table: which lane a module belongs to, and which lane
crossings a client bundle may not contain.
Both module graphs decide this, and a project is compiled by whichever one
the command it ran uses:
- crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/references.rs  (`build`, `check`, `preview`)
- packages/ruvyxa/runtime/compiler.mjs     (`dev`, and the SSG render path)
They had disagreed, and the looser one was the one a developer looks at in a
browser. The Rust bundler assigns a lane from the leading directive and then
from the file stem, so `server.ts`, `server.js`, `server.mjs`, `action.ts`,
`actions.ts`, and any `'use server'` module are all server-side. The Node
graph matched one literal filename — `server.ts` — so `server.js` (the other
half of the documented convention), every action module, and every
`'use server'` module were compiled into the browser bundle under
`ruvyxa dev` while `ruvyxa build` refused the same import with RUV1820.
Server-only source was served to a browser during development and could not
ship, which is the worst ordering: the leak is visible only where nobody
checks, and the error arrives only at the end.
Every implementation replays this file:
- crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/references.rs        (Rust test)
- tests/packages/ruvyxa/module-lane.test.mjs     (JavaScript test)
Add a case here first when changing what marks a module server-side.
$directiveNote: A leading directive wins over the filename: a `server.ts` that opens with
`'use client'` is a client module that happens to be named server. The
directive is read after a BOM, whitespace, and leading comments, and never
from text inside a later function or string.
$stemNote: Read from the file stem — the basename with its last extension removed — so
the rule does not depend on which language a project writes. `server.d.ts`
has the stem `server.d` and is not a server module.
The stem rule is a project convention and stops at an installed package.
`react-dom/server.js` is a package entry point a browser bundle may
legitimately contain; reading the convention into `node_modules` refused it,
and the adapter-runner suite caught that within one build. A directive still
counts wherever it appears — a dependency that declares `'use server'` means
$closureNote: A client boundary owns its shared dependency closure: a shared module
reachable from a client module is itself client. Server and action modules
terminate that closure rather than joining it, which is what makes the
crossing below detectable instead of silently absorbed.
The Node graph reaches the same answer from the other side: it compiles the
client closure and no more, so every module it sees on the browser platform
is already in that closure and only the module's own lane has to be checked.
$crossingNote: `actionToClient` is enforced by the Rust bundler alone. The Node graph has
no hook on the server compile that could see it, so this table records the
gap rather than implying a parity that does not exist. Both hosts enforce
`clientToServer` and `clientToAction`, which are the crossings that decide
whether server-only source reaches a browser.
$serverDirNote: Separate from the lane table and older than it: any file under the
project-level `server/` directory is server-side whatever it is named.
`ruvyxa_graph` reports it as RUV1010 and the Node graph as RUV1007.
$markerNote: Packages that exist only to be imported, and must never appear in emitted
`server-only` and `client-only` ship no runtime behaviour: importing one is a
declaration for the boundary checker, which has already run by the time a
bundle is written. Both linkers used to carry the import through into the
output anyway -- the Rust one re-emits any specifier it did not inline, and
the Node one hoisted it into a namespace import -- so a deployed function
directory, which has no node_modules of its own, failed to start with
ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for a package whose whole purpose was to not be there.
The application was a correct one: an RSC page that declares `server-only` is
exactly what the marker is for.

cases.$why: A directive marks a module even when the name says nothing.
Leading comments and a BOM precede a real directive.
cases.source:
﻿// header
/* block */
'use server'
export const q = 1

cases.$why: A directive-looking string that is not the prologue marks nothing.
An installed package named server is a package entry point, not a server module.
A dependency that declares a directive still means it.
